title: THE MAN WHO WROTE GOD’S WARNING WHILE A KING TRIED TO SILENCE IT
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO WROTE GOD’S WARNING WHILE A KING TRIED TO SILENCE IT
His name was Baruch. He wasn't the prophet. He wasn't the king. But when God's Word was rejected, his trembling hands helped preserve a message that would outlive the throne.
What if the greatest thing God ever asks you to do is something the world will never applaud?
What if your name never appears on a stage?
What if nobody remembers the sacrifices you made, the tears you cried, the nights you stayed awake, or the battles you fought just to remain faithful?
What if you spend your life helping someone else fulfill the calling God placed upon them?
Would you still obey?
Before you answer, I want you to meet a man whose story is buried in one of the most heartbreaking confrontations between God's mercy and human rebellion.
His name was Baruch.
And his story begins with a scroll, a prophet under restriction, a nation approaching disaster, and a king who would eventually take a knife to the very words God had sent to save his people.
But here is what makes this story so unsettling.
The king had the power to destroy the scroll.
He did not have the power to destroy the truth.
And the man holding the pen would discover that faithfulness to God does not always protect you from suffering.
Sometimes, it leads you directly into it.
If you have ever served God while feeling invisible, exhausted, unappreciated, or afraid, stay with this story.
Because Baruch's life may reveal something about your own that you have never considered.
And before we reach the end, we will encounter a promise God gave this overlooked servant—a promise that may change the way you understand success, survival, and the cost of following Jesus.
It was the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, around 605 BC.
Jerusalem was living on borrowed time.
The people still had their religious institutions. The temple still stood. Religious activity continued.
But beneath the appearance of spiritual security, the nation was drifting toward judgment.
For years, Jeremiah had warned Judah to turn from evil, abandon false confidence, and return to the Lord.
His warnings were not popular.
Truth rarely feels comforting when it confronts the sins we have learned to excuse.
Then God gave Jeremiah an extraordinary command.
In Jeremiah 36:2–3, the Lord instructed him to take a scroll and write the words He had spoken concerning Israel, Judah, and the nations. The purpose was not merely to announce punishment.
God declared that perhaps the people of Judah would hear of the disaster He intended, turn from their evil ways, and receive His forgiveness.
Read that carefully.
God sent a warning because He was still calling people to repentance.
The message of judgment was also an expression of mercy.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 36:3 contains a phrase worth remembering:
וְשָׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה
Ve-shavu ish mi-darko ha-ra'ah.
Meaning, in context, “and each one may turn from his evil way.”
The verb shuv (שׁוּב) carries the sense of turning or returning. In prophetic passages such as this, it describes a moral and spiritual turning away from evil.
Repentance was not presented as a religious performance.
It meant changing direction.
And the verse continued with God's promise to forgive their iniquity and sin.
There it was.
Judgment was approaching, but mercy was still being offered.
God was not telling Judah that rebellion did not matter.
He was telling them that their rebellion did matter—and that they needed to turn before destruction came.
That is the context in which Baruch entered the story.
Jeremiah 36:4 records that Jeremiah called Baruch, the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll the words the Lord had spoken to Jeremiah, as Jeremiah dictated them.
His name in Hebrew was:
בָּרוּךְ בֶּן־נֵרִיָּה
Barukh ben-Neriyyah.
Baruch, son of Neriah.
The name Baruch means “blessed.”
But being blessed by God did not mean his life would be easy.
Baruch was a scribe—a man capable of recording written documents. In the ancient world, scribal work required literacy and training, skills not universally possessed.
He was also associated with Jeremiah's prophetic ministry.
Jeremiah received the prophetic message from the Lord.
Baruch wrote it down as Jeremiah dictated.
That distinction matters.
Baruch was not inventing prophecies, speaking on his own authority, or secretly rewriting Jeremiah's message.
He was serving as the prophet's scribe.
And sometimes the most sacred responsibility God entrusts to someone is not creating a message of their own, but faithfully preserving the message He has already given.
Imagine the scene.
Jeremiah speaks.
Baruch listens.
The writing instrument moves across the scroll.
Sentence after sentence.
Warning after warning.
The sins of the nation are exposed. The consequences of rebellion are announced. The call to repentance remains.
And Baruch keeps writing.
He cannot soften the message simply because people may dislike it.
He cannot remove the uncomfortable passages.
He cannot make the warning more fashionable.
He must be faithful to what he has been given.
There is a lesson here for every Christian living in an age when biblical truth is sometimes reshaped to gain acceptance.
We are not authorized to change God's Word to make obedience more convenient.
But neither are we authorized to use God's Word as an excuse for cruelty.
The same Scripture that exposes sin reveals the mercy of the God who calls sinners to return.
Truth and grace are not enemies.
They meet perfectly in Jesus Christ.
And Baruch's story helps us understand why the written Word matters.
Because the message was never supposed to end with the person who first heard it.
Jeremiah could not personally enter the house of the Lord at that time. Jeremiah 36:5 describes him as restricted, although the passage does not specify the precise nature of that restriction.
So he gave Baruch another assignment.
He was to take the scroll into the temple and read the words publicly.
Not quietly to a trusted friend.
Not privately to a sympathetic audience.
But openly, before people who desperately needed to hear the truth.
Jeremiah 36:6 instructed Baruch to read the words from the scroll in the Lord's house on a day of fasting.
Then Jeremiah explained the hope behind the assignment.
Perhaps the people would bring their plea before the Lord.
Perhaps they would turn from their evil ways.
The anger and wrath pronounced against them were great.
But the call to repentance remained.
Think about what Baruch was being asked to do.
He was not simply copying religious literature.
He was becoming the public voice of a message that challenged the spiritual condition of his nation.
He would be associated with a prophet whose warnings had provoked resistance.
And he was entering a situation where obedience could become dangerous.
Would you have gone?
Would I?
It is easy to say we would stand for biblical truth when we imagine ourselves surrounded by people who agree with us.
It becomes harder when telling the truth might cost us relationships, opportunities, comfort, or security.
Sometimes we are willing to follow Jesus as long as obedience does not disturb the life we have carefully built.
But the Gospel never promised a comfortable path.
Jesus said in Luke 9:23 that anyone who would come after Him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Him.
That does not mean every difficulty we experience is persecution.
It does mean discipleship cannot be reduced to seeking personal convenience.
Baruch's obedience was not glamorous.
It was costly service.
And Jeremiah 36:8 gives us one of the simplest and most powerful descriptions of his character.
Baruch did everything Jeremiah commanded him concerning the reading of the Lord's words in the temple.
No dramatic speech about his own greatness.
No record of demanding recognition.
No insistence that his name receive equal prominence.
He obeyed.
And sometimes obedience is the most powerful testimony a person can give.
But the story did not end at verse eight.
And if we stop there, we miss the terrifying moment that reveals why Baruch's faithfulness mattered so much.
In the following events of Jeremiah 36, Baruch publicly read the scroll, and its contents eventually reached the royal court.
Officials heard the message and recognized its seriousness.
They questioned Baruch about how the words had been written.
He explained that Jeremiah had dictated them and he had written them with ink on the scroll.
The officials then told Baruch and Jeremiah to hide.
Why?
Because the message was moving toward the king.
And the king was not a man who welcomed correction.
Jehoiakim eventually heard the scroll read.
It was winter.
He was sitting in his winter house, with a fire burning before him.
And as portions of the scroll were read, the king cut them off with a scribe's knife and threw them into the fire.
Again.
And again.
Until the scroll was consumed.
Jeremiah 36:23 describes the destruction.
Imagine that moment.
The words of warning had reached the highest authority in the land.
The king had an opportunity to humble himself.
He could have listened.
He could have repented.
He could have acknowledged the seriousness of Judah's rebellion.
Instead, he destroyed the written message.
Jeremiah 36:24 adds a devastating detail.
Neither the king nor the servants who heard the words were afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
The scroll burned.
But the greater tragedy was not the destruction of parchment.
It was the hardness of the hearts listening.
A person can hear God's warning clearly and still refuse to surrender.
That is frightening.
Because spiritual danger does not always look like open hatred of God.
Sometimes it looks like hearing His Word repeatedly while refusing to let it change us.
We know what Scripture says about forgiveness, yet we continue nurturing bitterness.
We know what Jesus teaches about honesty, yet we keep protecting our secret compromises.
We know the call to repentance, yet we tell ourselves we will change someday.
We may never take a knife to a biblical manuscript.
But we can resist the authority of Scripture by refusing to obey what we understand.
The king destroyed the scroll because he did not want to submit to its message.
And the question reaches across the centuries.
What are we doing with the truth God has already placed before us?
Are we receiving it?
Or are we quietly cutting away the parts that confront us?
The story grows even more remarkable.
Jehoiakim commanded that Baruch and Jeremiah be seized.
But Jeremiah 36:26 records that the Lord hid them.
Scripture does not explain every detail of how God protected them.
It simply tells us that He did.
And then something happened that the king could not prevent.
God instructed Jeremiah to take another scroll and write again the words that had been on the first.
Jeremiah called Baruch.
Baruch wrote the words once more.
Jeremiah 36:32 tells us that many similar words were also added.
The first scroll was destroyed.
The prophetic message was not silenced.
The king's fire could consume the material on which the words were written.
It could not cancel the authority of the God who had spoken.
There is something deeply moving about Baruch returning to his work.
We are not told every emotion he experienced.
We cannot honestly claim to know whether his hands trembled, whether he wept, or whether he questioned what would happen next.
The biblical account does not describe those details.
But we know this.
He wrote again.
After the danger.
After the rejection.
After the king burned the scroll.
He wrote again.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear what that kind of faithfulness can teach us.
You may have tried to do what was right and watched everything fall apart.
You may have poured your heart into serving others and received little gratitude.
You may have spoken truth with love and still been rejected.
You may have prayed for someone who continued walking away from God.
You may be exhausted from trying to remain faithful when the results seem painfully small.
Baruch's story does not promise that every lost opportunity will return or that every earthly dream will be restored.
But it does remind us that the visible response to our obedience is not the final measure of its value.
Faithfulness belongs to us.
The outcome belongs to God.
And Baruch himself would need to learn that lesson in a deeply personal way.
Because there was another side to his story.
One that reveals he was not merely a courageous servant untouched by fear or disappointment.
He was human.
In Jeremiah 45, God addressed Baruch personally.
The chapter is dated to the same fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch had written Jeremiah's words on a scroll.
And what we discover is startling.
Baruch was hurting.
Jeremiah 45:3 records his lament, including the words:
“Woe is me now!”
He spoke of sorrow, groaning, and finding no rest.
This is the man who faithfully wrote the prophetic message.
The man who served beside Jeremiah.
The man whose obedience placed him in the middle of a national spiritual crisis.
And he was weary.
Not every faithful servant feels strong.
Not every believer who speaks courageously in public feels courageous in private.
Some people carry the Word of God to others while struggling under burdens nobody sees.
They encourage their families while privately grieving.
They serve in ministry while fighting discouragement.
They remind others of God's promises while wondering how they themselves will make it through another difficult season.
If that describes you, Baruch's story is not permission to abandon obedience.
But it is evidence that Scripture does not hide the emotional struggles of God's servants.
God knew Baruch's distress.
And God spoke to him.
But His response was not merely the reassurance Baruch might have expected.
Jeremiah 45:5 records a piercing question:
“And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not.” (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
וְאַתָּה תְבַקֶּשׁ־לְךָ גְדֹלוֹת
Ve-attah tevaqqesh-lekha gedolot.
“And you, are you seeking great things for yourself?”
The Hebrew emphasizes the personal nature of the question.
God was confronting Baruch's pursuit of greatness for himself in a time when judgment was coming upon the land.
We are not told precisely what those great things were.
We should not invent ambitions the passage does not identify.
But the warning is clear.
Baruch needed to reconsider what he was seeking.
God was about to bring disaster upon the land, and Baruch was not to measure his future by the pursuit of personal greatness.
Instead, God promised that wherever Baruch went, He would give him his life as a prize of war.
It was a promise of preservation amid catastrophe.
Not a guarantee of wealth.
Not a promise of public recognition.
Not an assurance that suffering would disappear.
His life would be spared.
And that was a gift.
What a difficult but necessary lesson.
Sometimes we ask God to make our names great when He is calling us to make His name known.
Sometimes we want the platform more than the obedience.
The recognition more than the responsibility.
The blessing more than the One who blesses.
And sometimes God, in His mercy, confronts the ambitions that are quietly taking possession of our hearts.
Baruch was called blessed by name.
Yet the blessing God promised him was not the kind of greatness people normally celebrate.
It was life preserved through judgment.
That should challenge the way we define success.
Because in the kingdom of God, being known by the Lord matters more than being admired by the world.
And this is where Baruch's story begins to point us toward someone infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ.
Baruch was a faithful scribe who recorded a prophetic warning.
Jesus is the eternal Word who became flesh.
John 1:1 declares:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “Word” is:
λόγος — Logos.
And John 1:14 declares that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Baruch wrote words entrusted to Jeremiah.
Jesus did not merely write or carry a message from God.
He is God the Son, who entered human history to reveal the Father and accomplish our redemption.
We must not confuse their roles.
Baruch was a servant.
Jesus is the Savior.
Baruch helped preserve a warning that called Judah to repentance.
Jesus came to accomplish the salvation to which the Scriptures ultimately bear witness.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
A king in Jeremiah's day rejected God's warning and burned the scroll.
Centuries later, the promised Messiah would also face rejection from human authorities.
But Jesus would not simply survive His enemies.
He would willingly go to the cross.
He would bear the sins of His people.
He would die.
And on the third day, He would rise again.
The resurrection was not merely a recovery from defeat.
It was the decisive victory of the crucified and risen Lord over sin and death.
And here is where the message becomes painfully personal.
The greatest danger in your life is not that someone might reject your achievements.
It is that you might reject the Savior who came to rescue you.
Because the Gospel does not tell us that we are basically good people who only need a little encouragement.
It tells us that we are sinners who need forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so no one may boast.
Do you see the beauty?
The answer to our guilt is not pretending we have never sinned.
The answer is not hiding our failures beneath religious appearances.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
His sacrifice.
His mercy.
His righteousness.
His resurrection.
And the invitation to repent and believe.
The Hebrew call to turn from evil in Jeremiah 36 finds a profound Gospel resonance in the preaching of Jesus.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
It calls for repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling sorry after being caught.
It is not making promises to God while deliberately planning to continue in rebellion.
True repentance involves a changed orientation toward sin and toward the Lord.
And even repentance is not a way to purchase forgiveness.
We come to Christ empty-handed, depending on His mercy.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is insignificant.
But that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself to redeem sinners who could never save themselves.
And grace does not leave those who receive it unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus erases every consequence of our past.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not because Christians never struggle again.
But because the risen Christ forgives sinners, gives them new life, and brings them into a future defined by His redeeming mercy rather than by the final authority of their past failures.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to be the master of your future.
Your sin must be confessed, not defended.
Your shame can be brought into the light of Christ.
Your failures do not make you beyond the reach of His mercy.
And your life, however ordinary it may appear, can become an instrument of faithfulness in His hands.
Baruch did not need a throne to matter.
He needed to obey the Lord.
And perhaps that is the word your heart has been avoiding.
You keep waiting for a greater opportunity before becoming faithful with the one already in front of you.
You keep comparing your assignment with someone else's calling.
You keep wondering whether your service matters because nobody seems to notice.
But the kingdom of God is not built only through the people whose names are remembered.
It is also served by those who pray when nobody is watching.
Those who teach children the Scriptures.
Those who care for aging parents.
Those who refuse dishonest gain.
Those who forgive when bitterness would be easier.
Those who share the Gospel with one frightened soul.
Those who give generously without demanding recognition.
Those who quietly keep showing up.
And those who, like Baruch, continue doing what God has entrusted to them even when the world seems determined not to listen.
Maybe your assignment is not to stand before thousands.
Maybe it is to speak truth gently to one person who is drifting away from Jesus.
Maybe it is to return to prayer after months of spiritual dryness.
Maybe it is to confess a hidden sin.
Maybe it is to reconcile with someone you have wounded.
Maybe it is to stop seeking admiration and begin seeking faithfulness.
Whatever the Lord is calling you to do, do not despise obedience simply because it looks small.
The God who saw Baruch sees His servants today.
And He does not need the world's applause to know whether we have been faithful.
There is another reason this story matters in our generation.
We live in a world overflowing with messages.
Millions of words are written, posted, shared, and forgotten.
People are surrounded by information while often starving for wisdom.
A person can spend hours consuming content and still go to sleep spiritually empty.
We can know the latest controversy, recognize every celebrity, and remember every argument on social media while struggling to recall the words of Jesus.
But the Word of God is not disposable content.
It is not merely another opinion competing for attention.
Second Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, equipping God's servant for good works.
And Hebrews 4:12 describes the Word of God as living and active.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture religious excitement.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to build a personality around human applause.
But to help place Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and the message of Jesus Christ before people who desperately need the truth.
Some are believers growing weary.
Some are Christians who have become spiritually distracted.
Some are struggling with secret sin.
Some have been wounded by others and are trying to understand the difference between human failure and the faithfulness of God.
Some have never truly understood the Gospel.
And some may be one honest conversation away from opening the Bible again.
This is why sharing a Christ-centered message can matter.
You do not know what someone is carrying behind the photograph they posted today.
You do not know which friend is questioning whether God could forgive them.
You do not know which family member is silently wrestling with shame.
You do not know who needs to be reminded that repentance is still possible and that Christ's mercy is greater than their ability to repair themselves.
Not to impress anyone with your spirituality.
Not to prove you are a better Christian.
But because truth worth receiving is often worth passing along.
Send this to someone who has grown tired of doing good.
And if Baruch's struggle exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to do something more personal.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to let fellow believers know that someone needs prayer.
Someone else may need the encouragement your story can provide.
Not because every sentence is something you must remember.
But because the biblical passages behind this story are worth returning to when faithfulness feels difficult.
Read Jeremiah 36 for yourself.
Then read Jeremiah 45.
Read them slowly.
Notice the mercy in God's warning.
Notice the courage required of His servants.
Notice the danger of rejecting correction.
And notice how God addressed the hidden struggles of a man whose work helped preserve His message.
Let Scripture speak more loudly than the article that introduced you to it.
And if you have been blessed by this ministry, there is another way you can participate in helping its work continue.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical encouragement and discipleship resources accessible to people who need them.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become better equipped to follow Christ.
Maintaining, developing, and expanding ministry resources takes time, effort, and practical support.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in a work you believe is worth sustaining.
But I want to be especially clear about something important.
Christians should give thoughtfully, freely, and responsibly, including honoring their commitments to their local churches and those in genuine need.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not a payment for God's favor.
Not a purchase of spiritual blessing.
Not a requirement for becoming a faithful Christian.
And certainly not a substitute for repentance, faith, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, or the life of the local church.
The Gospel is free because Jesus paid the price we could never pay.
Our financial support does not make us more worthy of His love.
We give because we have received grace, not because we are trying to buy it.
And whether or not you are able to contribute financially, you can still make a meaningful difference.
Invite someone to read Jeremiah 36.
Pray that the message of Jesus Christ would reach people whose hearts are ready to hear it.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth in God's kingdom.
The invitation to receive the Gospel is not behind a payment wall.
The invitation to help sustain this ministry is simply an opportunity for those who are willing and able.
And perhaps that is a fitting lesson from Baruch.
Not everyone is called to the same assignment.
Not everyone has the same resources.
Not everyone serves in the same way.
But every believer can seek to honor Christ with what has been entrusted to them.
A voice.
A prayer.
A gift.
A word of encouragement.
A quiet act of obedience.
A willingness to share truth.
A life surrendered to Jesus.
Now, before you leave this story, I want to bring you back to that winter room in Jerusalem.
A king sits beside a fire.
A scroll is read.
The warning of God reaches his ears.
He takes a knife.
He cuts.
He burns.
And for a moment, it might appear that the king has won.
The message is reduced to ashes.
The servants of God are threatened.
The voice of warning seems silenced.
But somewhere beyond the reach of that royal fire, the Lord's purpose continues.
Another scroll will be written.
Another opportunity to preserve the prophetic words will be given.
And Baruch, the overlooked scribe, will take up his work again.
The king's name remains in Scripture as a warning.
Baruch's name remains as the record of a servant who faithfully wrote what he was given.
Yet even Baruch's faithfulness is not the center of the Christian story.
Jesus is.
Because our hope is not that we can become strong enough to save ourselves through obedience.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has done what we could never do.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So perhaps the most important question is not whether you will ever be remembered like Baruch.
Perhaps it is whether you have surrendered your life to the Savior to whom all Scripture ultimately directs us.
Have you been resisting God's correction?
Have you been hiding behind religious activity while avoiding repentance?
Have you been seeking great things for yourself while neglecting the One who gave Himself for you?
Have you allowed disappointment to convince you that quiet faithfulness is worthless?
Then hear the invitation of Christ.
Come to Him.
Not with a performance.
Not with a carefully edited version of your past.
Not with the illusion that you can earn your way into His favor.
Come confessing your need for mercy.
Come trusting His finished work.
Come ready to follow Him.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse from unrighteousness.
And John 6:37 records Jesus' promise that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
There is room for the repentant sinner at the feet of Jesus.
There is forgiveness for those who turn to Him in faith.
There is grace for the weary servant.
And there is a calling for the believer who has forgotten that obedience matters even when nobody applauds.
Baruch's pen reminds us that one faithful act can become part of a story far greater than the servant can see.
But Christ's cross reminds us of something greater still.
Our salvation rests not in the greatness of our service, but in the greatness of our Savior.
So do not merely admire Baruch.
Learn from him.
Do not merely fear Jehoiakim's hard heart.
Examine your own.
Do not merely celebrate that God's message survived the fire.
Receive the truth it proclaims.
And above everything else, look to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not being forgotten by the world.
It is hearing the call of Christ and refusing the grace He offers.
Surrender to Jesus.
Trust His grace.
Follow His Word.
And remember this:
The world may never remember the hands that served in secret, but the Savior who bore the scars of your redemption will never overlook a life surrendered to Him.
